routes.description: Infer Jesus's bodily resurrection as the best explanation of his death, empty tomb, and reported appearances.
routes.successCriteria: Establish the three historical facts with adequate independence and show bodily resurrection explains them better than live alternatives.

motionBridge.description: The historical evidence establishes that Jesus physically rose from the dead.

centralBridges.description: Death by crucifixion, an empty tomb, and sincere appearance beliefs are strongly evidenced historical facts.
Bodily resurrection explains the three facts better than plausible alternatives.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Early creedal and Pauline material expresses bodily resurrection rather than merely spiritual survival.
Historical and medical considerations make survival of crucifixion unlikely.

routes.description: Argue that the sources do not establish either certain death on the cross or a bodily postmortem reappearance.
routes.successCriteria: Show that decisive premises of the resurrection inference depend on later, developing accounts or otherwise admit materially plausible alternatives.

motionBridge.description: The historical evidence does not establish that Jesus physically rose from the dead.

centralBridges.description: Increasingly physical Gospel details reflect development and cannot simply be aggregated as independent history.
The delivered evidence does not establish that Jesus was certainly dead before removal from the cross.
Early resurrection belief does not establish a physical bodily appearance.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Paul's appearance and resurrection language can be read without the later physical details.
Differences among appearance narratives weaken their use as cumulative physical evidence.

sections.title: The three facts and best-explanation inference
sections.rationale: This is the pro side's explicit motion-level case and fixes the central evidential burden for the debate.

proMoves.speaker: Michael Licona
proMoves.proposition: Jesus's death, empty tomb, and appearance beliefs are strongly evidenced, and resurrection is the best explanation absent a plausible alternative.

sourceSpan.excerpt: three facts then this evening number one Jesus death by crucifixion number two the empty tomb and number three the appearances to both friend and foe ... in the absence of any plausible alternate theories to account for these facts Jesus resurrection can be accepted with confidence

proMoves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly gives Licona the opening statement, and this uninterrupted span concludes it.

response.rationale: This is the initial complete affirmative inference and has no earlier selected target.

precisionFindings.rationale: The three premises, comparative standard, and historical conclusion are expressly stated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move invokes strong evidence, scholarly uptake, and best explanation, but compresses independence and rival-hypothesis testing.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The abductive route is clear, though the transition from accepted data to occurrence relies on a compressed comparative bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specific historical considerations and claimed scholarly agreement support the facts, but representativeness and full comparison with alternatives remain compressed.

responsiveness.rationale: As a constructive opening, it directly advances a complete and intelligible case.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It supports the complete motion-level conclusion proportionately.

representationalCharity.rationale: No developed live alternative is represented in this selected opening span.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: Ledger events 204-218 state the three facts, their evidential status, the explanatory inference, and the burden placed on the opposing side.

conMoves.speaker: Shabir Ally
conMoves.proposition: Early belief that Jesus was alive with God does not itself establish bodily resurrection or an empty tomb.

sourceSpan.excerpt: the evidence which you have cited showing that there was an early acknowledgment that Jesus reappeared to his disciples ... does not necessitate his bodily Resurrection ... that conclusion does not necessitate finding his tomb empty and knowing that he physically bodily resurrected from the dead

conMoves.attributionBasis: Licona asks a direct question and Ally supplies the uninterrupted answer.

components.text: Challenges the inference from early appearance belief to bodily resurrection and an empty tomb.
Does not answer the death-by-crucifixion component in this span.
Does not comparatively establish a complete alternative explanation of all three facts.

response.rationale: It directly contacts a decisive appearance-to-body inference but not every indispensable component of the three-fact case.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is expressly limited to what early belief does not necessitate.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move argues underdetermination and expressly offers a possible nonbodily interpretation rather than certainty.

charity.alternative: Licona's early evidence is treated as evidence of sincere resurrection belief and appearances.
charity.decisiveQualification: Ally distinguishes that acknowledged belief from proof of bodily reanimation and an empty tomb.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The non-entailment is coherent, though the analogy to Abraham and Moses only partly fits claims that include burial and appearance language.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual distinction is relevant, but the proposed spiritual reading receives limited textual demonstration in this span.

responsiveness.rationale: It contacts a decisive component of the target but leaves death and comparative explanation unanswered.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It materially attacks the central factual bridge of the pro route.

representationalCharity.rationale: It acknowledges early belief and reported appearances before contesting their bodily implication.

conMoves.evidenceBasis: Ledger events 427-438 distinguish early belief in survival with God from bodily resurrection and an empty tomb.

sections.title: Whether the earliest tradition entails bodily resurrection
sections.rationale: This exchange directly tests whether evidence predating the Gospels supplies the physicality needed by the motion.

proMoves.speaker: Michael Licona
proMoves.proposition: Early creeds and Pauline material repeatedly say Jesus died and was raised, while ancient resurrection meant the buried body was raised and transformed.

sourceSpan.excerpt: when we go back to the earliest tradition like for example the Creeds ... that he died that he was raised ... James DG Dunn says that the Creed in 1 Corinthians 15 dates to within months of the crucifixion ... the body that was buried is the same body that's raised and was transformed into an immortal body

proMoves.attributionBasis: The speaker change follows Ally's answer, and Licona explicitly takes issue before presenting his reply.

components.text: Cites early creed and Pauline death-and-raised language.
Argues that resurrection in the relevant ancient context denoted transformation of the buried body.

response.rationale: It answers both the asserted lateness problem and the claimed gap between resurrection language and bodily resurrection.

precisionFindings.rationale: The route is clear, but broad claims about the ancient concept of resurrection leave some contextual variation implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The numerous early references support the position, but the move treats the semantic inference as more uniform than it demonstrates.

charity.alternative: Ally's view is represented as allowing early belief while denying that it necessitates bodily resurrection.
charity.decisiveQualification: Licona targets the decisive qualification by arguing that the early term itself carried bodily content.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The chronology-plus-semantics reply forms a stable route with a bounded contextual assumption.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: It supplies named texts, frequency, dating, and a semantic warrant, though source independence and semantic variation remain compressed.

responsiveness.rationale: It explicitly contacts both indispensable parts of the earlier underdetermination claim.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move supports the declared subsidiary bridge concerning early bodily tradition.

representationalCharity.rationale: It accurately identifies Ally's distinction before directly disputing it.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: Ledger events 439-454 contain the early-creed dating, Pauline references, and bodily-resurrection semantic argument.

conMoves.speaker: Shabir Ally
conMoves.proposition: Paul does not identify the source of the creeds, and Paul's own inclusion among the appearances makes a nonphysical visionary reading possible.

sourceSpan.excerpt: Paul does not say where he got these from and Paul in adding his own self ... to the list of people to whom Jesus appeared is adding ... a person to whom Jesus appeared somehow spiritually ... none of the evidence you have cited actually proves that Jesus physically bodily rose from the dead

conMoves.attributionBasis: This is Ally's immediate answer to Licona's early-tradition argument.

components.text: Challenges the unstated provenance of the creedal formulas.
Uses Paul's inclusion and Acts' light narrative to support possible visionary appearances.
Does not directly rebut the claimed ancient bodily meaning of resurrection.

response.rationale: It contests provenance and appearance mode but leaves the principal semantic argument incompletely answered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The possibility claim is clear, but 'spiritual' and 'non-physical' are used without a fully fixed distinction from visionary experience.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move properly frames its alternative as something the evidence cannot preclude.

charity.alternative: Licona's argument from early creeds and numerous Pauline resurrection references is substantially acknowledged.
charity.decisiveQualification: Ally notes that early dating and repeated language do not by themselves settle provenance or appearance mode.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The visionary possibility is intelligible, though moving from Paul's experience to the others is analogical and not independently established.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Acts' description and Paul's inclusion give relevant support, but the generalization to prior witnesses remains speculative.

responsiveness.rationale: It contacts the appearance-mode component decisively but does not answer the semantic claim about resurrection.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It attacks the declared subsidiary bridge concerning early bodily tradition.

representationalCharity.rationale: It engages the actual early-material argument, with only limited compression of Licona's semantic warrant.

conMoves.evidenceBasis: Ledger events 455-470 state the provenance objection, Paul's light appearance, and the nonphysical possibility.

sections.title: Whether death on the cross is sufficiently established
sections.rationale: Actual death is indispensable to a resurrection inference and becomes a sustained, directly contested factual issue.

proMoves.speaker: Michael Licona
proMoves.proposition: Uniform testimony, the nature of crucifixion, medical judgment, and scholarly consensus strongly establish Jesus's death despite uncertainty about the exact physiological mechanism.

sourceSpan.excerpt: everybody attests to it our understanding of crucifixion militates against it and medically the doctors are saying he died ... except for the Romantic few who think that Jesus did not die on the cross most Scholars accept the uniform testimony of the gospels that Jesus died during the Judean prefecture of Pontius Pilate

proMoves.attributionBasis: Licona explicitly responds after Ally asks for evidence that Jesus actually died.

components.text: Answers with uniform Gospel testimony and broad scholarly acceptance.
Invokes medical judgment and the lethal character of crucifixion.
Does not fully answer the specific short-duration and sympathetic-Pilate survival scenario.

response.rationale: It supplies strong general contrary evidence but incompletely addresses the opponent's case-specific survival mechanism.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conclusion is clear and distinguished from certainty about the exact cause of death.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move claims strong historical support, not absolute proof, and acknowledges the physiological dispute.

charity.alternative: Ally's survival contention is treated as the view that Jesus did not die despite crucifixion testimony.
charity.decisiveQualification: The reply acknowledges uncertainty over physiological cause but argues that this does not negate death.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between uncertain mechanism and well-supported outcome is sound, though consensus is not itself the complete causal warrant.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move supplies multiple evidence types and a specific Brown passage, with a residual gap on the case-specific survival scenario.

responsiveness.rationale: It contacts attestation and medical components but only partially answers the specific short-crucifixion scenario.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It supports the declared subsidiary death-certainty bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: It fairly engages the nondeath claim, though it compresses Ally's narrower argument about this particular crucifixion.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: Ledger events 658-670 present the attestation, crucifixion, medical, and Raymond Brown consensus reply.

conMoves.speaker: Shabir Ally
conMoves.proposition: Mark's short crucifixion, Pilate's doubt and sympathy, and the late placement of the spear wound leave a plausible survival possibility.

sourceSpan.excerpt: the earliest strata of tradition cannot convince you that Jesus actually died on the cross ... in Mark's gospel Jesus was only on the cross for a few hours ... pilate was sympathetic towards Jesus ... it is possible that his men would not have delivered to Jesus the most brutal punishment possible

conMoves.attributionBasis: Ally explicitly enumerates his answer to Licona's first fact during their direct exchange.

components.text: Directly challenges the death premise with a case-specific survival scenario.
Does not answer the empty-tomb premise in this span.
Does not answer the appearance premise in this span.

response.rationale: It directly attacks one indispensable fact but not the remaining components of the complete inference.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is consistently framed as a possibility and as insufficiency of proof.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Short duration and textual details permit a hypothesis, but Pilate's sympathy is treated as extending to his men without direct support.

charity.alternative: Licona's death premise and reliance on historical and medical considerations are directly recognized.
charity.decisiveQualification: Ally narrows the objection to whether those general considerations establish death in this particular reported sequence.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The route is intelligible, but Pilate's sympathy to moderated punishment and survival requires several unsupported conditional links.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The short duration and textual variation are relevant, while the rescue cooperation and survival mechanism remain speculative.

responsiveness.rationale: It directly contacts the decisive death premise but not the other indispensable components of the overall target.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It materially advances the con route's central death-underdetermination bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: It addresses the actual death premise without denying that crucifixion generally could be lethal.

conMoves.evidenceBasis: Ledger events 607-630 give the short-duration, Pilate, punishment, spear-wound, and source-development contentions.

sections.title: Gospel development and appearance narratives
sections.rationale: The final decisive exchange tests whether differences between Luke, John, and Mark demonstrate legendary physical development.

proMoves.speaker: Michael Licona
proMoves.proposition: John need not be expanding the appearance tradition because Luke may instead compress a longer sequence into Easter day, with Acts supplying broader chronology.

sourceSpan.excerpt: I don't think John is so much is expanding as we have Luke Contracting in Luke's gospel ... it seems like everything happens in Jerusalem on Easter ... in Luke's sequel acts ... Jesus after having been raised he met them in Galilee ... John is not expanding in his gospel Luke is Contracting

proMoves.attributionBasis: Licona immediately answers Ally's explicit question about Luke and John.

components.text: Offers Luke's contraction as an alternative to John's expansion.
Does not directly reconcile Thomas's absence with Luke's presentation of the gathered disciples.
Attempts chronological support from Acts, but the cited wording is disputed within the exchange.

response.rationale: It offers an issue-bearing alternative redactional account but leaves the specific Thomas discrepancy unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: The contraction thesis is recoverable, but the claimed Acts chronology shifts during the ensuing textual discussion.

calibrationFindings.rationale: It is appropriately offered as an alternative, though the cited Acts text does not clearly state appearances in Galilee.

charity.alternative: Ally's claim that John expands Luke to create an additional physical appearance is accurately identified.
charity.decisiveQualification: Licona preserves the observed narrative difference but proposes contraction by Luke rather than invention by John.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Contraction is a coherent rival explanation, but the Acts support is textually uncertain and the Thomas detail remains untreated.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Luke's compressed narration gives some basis, while the crucial Acts reading is challenged and inadequately secured.

responsiveness.rationale: It contacts the redactional inference but does not answer the specific contradiction about Thomas.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It materially attacks the con route's central source-development bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: It represents the expansion claim fairly and offers a genuine rival reading.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: Ledger events 988-1009 contain the contraction thesis, Luke chronology, Acts citation, and claimed alternative explanation.

conMoves.speaker: Shabir Ally
conMoves.proposition: Luke depicts an Easter appearance to the gathered eleven, whereas John makes Thomas absent to create a later, more physically evidential appearance, indicating narrative development.

sourceSpan.excerpt: in The Gospel According to Luke Jesus appears to the 11 disciples on Easter day whereas in The Gospel according to John Thomas was absent ... John has deliberately worded it this way so that he can create a new event for the further appearance of Jesus ... John is expanding the story giving us more proof more physical hard evidence

conMoves.attributionBasis: The moderator gives Ally a final question to Licona, and Ally states this challenge directly.

components.text: Supplies a specific Gospel comparison suggesting later physical elaboration.
Does not directly rebut the dating or wording of the early creedal evidence.

response.rationale: It directly supports a development objection but does not answer the independent pre-Gospel evidence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The textual comparison is clear, but authorial deliberateness is asserted without qualification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: A narrative difference supports development as a possibility, but does not alone establish John's deliberate invention.

charity.alternative: Licona's case for physical appearances is engaged through the detailed Gospel narratives that appear to support it.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move argues that these details are later evidence rather than independent confirmation of the earliest belief.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The comparative observation supports a development hypothesis, but the inference to deliberate creation is not necessary.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: A concrete Luke-John difference is provided, while intentional invention and direction of dependence remain underwarranted.

responsiveness.rationale: It contacts later physical elaboration but not the early-creed component of the selected target.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It supports the declared subsidiary Gospel-discrepancy bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: It engages the strongest physical narrative evidence, though it compresses the independent early-material argument.

conMoves.evidenceBasis: Ledger events 981-987 state the Luke-John comparison, Thomas's absence, and the proposed expansion inference.
